label: Continuity Of Convex Functions
notes: Start by telling students that this section is less about epsilon bookkeeping and more about geometry removing options. A convex graph cannot make an isolated interior jump because every nearby point is tied to surrounding points by chords. Keep the contrast in view: relative interiors are rigid, while relative boundaries still allow approach-path surprises.

label: Interior Regularity
notes: Make Theorem 10.1 feel like a local theorem rather than a global miracle. The proof route can be summarized as lower semicontinuity from closure facts plus upper semicontinuity from the geometry of the epigraph. Students should hear that the relative-open hypothesis is doing real work by keeping a small convex testing zone around the point.

label: Relative Interior Domain
notes: Spend time on the word relative. Many functions in convex analysis live naturally on faces, affine images, or lower-dimensional feasible sets. The ambient ball may be useless there, but a relative ball inside the affine hull is enough. This is why the theorem is stated for relatively open convex sets rather than ordinary open sets only.

label: Local Boundedness
notes: Local boundedness is the quiet mechanism behind the polished continuity statements. In ordinary analysis, boundedness alone would be far too weak. Convexity changes the game because values at the sides of a small convex neighborhood control values between them. Emphasize that this mechanism needs a genuine neighborhood in the relevant affine hull.

label: Chords Control Oscillation
notes: Use the chord picture as the main intuition of the lecture. If a convex graph tried to jump at an interior point, chords from fixed surrounding points would have to bend in incompatible ways. The monotone secant-slope check is not a full proof, but it is the finite picture students should keep in mind when reading the theorem.

label: Lipschitz On Compact Cores
notes: Present Theorem 10.4 as the quantitative version of interior regularity. Once a compact set sits strictly inside the relative domain, there is room to extend a secant past one point and compare it to a bounded value on a buffer. The Lipschitz constant is therefore a geometric consequence of distance from the boundary.

label: Boundary Blow-up
notes: The boundary example should feel fair, not pathological for its own sake. Convexity still controls straight approaches from inside a fixed simplex, but it cannot compare every tangent approach to the same interior data. This is the moment to say that closedness gives lower semicontinuity, while upper semicontinuity at the boundary needs extra geometry.

label: Closed Versus Continuous
notes: Separate two properties that students often fuse together. A closed convex function has a closed epigraph, so it cannot suddenly fall below its limiting values. Continuity also requires it not to jump upward. Interior convexity supplies the missing upper control, but boundary points require additional hypotheses such as local simplicial structure or bounded extension data.

label: Continuity Under Sums
notes: Use sums as a first operation where qualification matters. Convexity of f plus g is easy, but continuity requires a place where both functions have real neighborhoods in their effective domains. The same pattern explains supremums and infimal projections: once the operation has produced a finite convex function on a relative-open region, the continuity theorem takes over.

label: Composition Warnings
notes: Composition is where students often overgeneralize the section. The continuity theorems apply after convexity and finite-domain hypotheses are secured; they do not make arbitrary compositions convex. Emphasize the safe affine case and then connect parameter continuity to the family theorem, where compactness in the parameter supplies the uniform bounds needed for joint continuity.

label: Epigraph View
notes: Re-enter epigraph language to connect this section with the previous closure material. The point is not to reproduce the printed proof line by line, but to name the moves: lower semicontinuity comes from closed epigraph behavior, and upper semicontinuity comes from open strict sublevel sets obtained by slicing and projecting the epigraph over an interior domain.

label: Numerical Modulus Check
notes: Treat the JSON check as a tiny lab notebook rather than evidence for the infinite theorem. It gives students a way to audit the idea on a familiar convex function: sample secants, compute ratios, and compare them with a core Lipschitz bound. Then remind them that the theorem supplies the missing continuum argument.

label: Failure Gallery
notes: Run the gallery like a diagnostic quiz. For each panel, ask which hypothesis has been removed and what the theorem can no longer conclude. This keeps counterexamples from feeling random. The point is that convexity is powerful but not omnipotent; it needs the right domain, closure, and uniformity data to become continuity.

label: Rule Ledger
notes: The ledger is the final operational memory for the lecture. Read each row from left to right: identify the construction, state the qualification, then name the continuity conclusion. The inspection prompt is the habit students should take into later sections, especially duality arguments where closures and domain qualifications decide whether operations behave cleanly.

label: Recap
notes: Close by returning to the sentence that convexity makes interior continuity inevitable but boundary continuity conditional. Ask students to name the available buffer, chord, or uniform bound before applying any continuity result. That gives them a portable method for later material: never invoke a closure or operation theorem without first locating the relative-interior core.
